title: Decentralized Role Assignment in Multi-Agent Teams via Empirical Game-Theoretic Analysis
abstract_summary: A robot picks its own role on the team without communicating with teammates, using only what it knows about the team's structure. Role assignment is modeled as a dynamic game and analyzed with empirical game theory, so each robot runs a distributed controller that switches among feedback policies over time. Simulations of collaborative planar manipulation show robots moving an object together while avoiding collisions.
conclusion_summary: The method gives heterogeneous teams a fully decentralized way to choose roles, and coordination emerged in 2D transport simulations, balancing each robot's preference against the team goal. The authors suggest the receding-horizon approach could extend to other multi-agent planning problems, such as choosing among several equilibria.
note: Just before the five-year window, but the closest match to the idea.

title: Distributed and Decentralized Control and Task Allocation for Flexible Swarms
abstract_summary: A bio-inspired swarm controller built from simple local rules. Agents are identical, anonymous, memoryless, short-sighted and cannot talk directly. A three-layer model (agent, formation, swarm) rests on cohesion, flexibility, attraction-repulsion and peristaltic motion. Broadcast steering signals create temporary "anonymous leaders" that pull the swarm toward unexplored areas with tasks.
conclusion_summary: Agents with limited sensing can search for tasks while staying connected, with no explicit coordination. Swarm speed depends on how many agents receive the steering signal. Future work is obstacle handling, relevant to search and rescue.

title: Graph-based Decentralized Task Allocation for Multi-Robot Target Localization
abstract_summary: GATAR is a decentralized graph attention model that assigns targets to a mixed team of ground and aerial robots. Robots share information with neighbors in communication range, so the team keeps working when members join, leave or fail. A preprocessing step handles differences between robot types so one shared model serves all. In simulation, allocations come close to an expert algorithm, with median spatial error under one grid unit.
conclusion_summary: One model can run different robot types thanks to the heterogeneity-aware preprocessing, with near-optimal results and good scaling across team sizes. Limits: it is not yet tied into upstream perception or downstream path planning. Future work is an end-to-end system, real-robot deployment, latency and use of historical collaboration data.

title: Task Allocation in Mobile Robot Fleets: A Review
abstract_summary: A survey of task allocation methods for fleets such as hospital or warehouse robots, including newer AI-based approaches. It summarizes simulation results and the software frameworks used to build them, then points out gaps.
conclusion_summary: AI-based allocation is an emerging trend. Two gaps stand out: few studies handle dynamic environments, and simulations are often too simplified for real deployment. Real-world experiments have been rare, so the authors call for more realistic simulation (with humans and moving obstacles) and physical tests.

title: Latent Theory of Mind: A Decentralized Diffusion Architecture for Cooperative Manipulation
authors: He, Schwager, Sznaier Camps, Liu, Sartoretti
abstract_summary: LatentToM is a decentralized diffusion policy for multi-arm manipulation. Each robot keeps a private (ego) representation and a shared consensus representation, and learns to predict the other robot's ego representation from its own consensus view, a latent-space version of theory of mind. A sheaf-inspired loss aligns the consensus representations. Execution can be fully distributed or use one communication round. On hardware it beats a naive decentralized baseline and matches a state-of-the-art centralized policy on bimanual tasks.
conclusion_summary: Combining sheaf-based consistency, theory of mind and directional consensus constraints balances coordination against expressiveness. Results are competitive with centralized baselines. The sheaf Laplacian can optionally be applied at inference time to improve stability without retraining. Scaling to larger robot teams is left for future work.

title: One Hand Watches The Other: Dynamic Multi-Agent Cooperation for Sample-Efficient Bimanual Manipulation in Dynamic Environments
abstract_summary: Multi-stream policies are data-efficient because they express actions relative to reference frames, but they assume those frames do not react to the robot's own actions. That fails when the robot moves an object or when two arms work together, since each arm becomes part of the other's changing environment. DynaMAC is a lightweight layer that treats the other arm as a dynamic task parameter, so bimanual coordination works without a fixed leader. On the new DynaBench benchmark it gains over 35 percentage points with 20 times fewer samples, and policies trained on static demonstrations transfer zero-shot to dynamic settings.
conclusion_summary: One framework covers moving objects, bimanual tasks and multi-agent cooperation with no explicit hierarchy or coordination module. Built on top of existing multi-stream policies, it keeps their sample efficiency and re-coordinates when either arm is perturbed. Limits: it needs segmentable skills and an external vision encoder. Future work is human-robot collaboration and whole-body mobile manipulation.

title: CLAS: Coordinating Multi-Robot Manipulation with Central Latent Action Spaces
abstract_summary: Reinforcement learning struggles with tasks like dual-arm manipulation because the action and state spaces grow large. Framing them as multi-agent problems helps, but decentralized agents then need a way to coordinate. The authors learn a shared, robot-agnostic latent action space focused on what matters for the task. Simulations show better learning efficiency and performance than earlier baselines.
conclusion_summary: Latent central action spaces coordinate decentralized agents. Training uses full observations and actions, while each robot acts independently at execution. The method beats the baselines, solves a four-arm lifting task that centralized approaches could not, and is more robust to disturbances.

title: DyDexHandover: Human-like Dynamic Dexterous Bimanual Handover using RGB-only Perception
abstract_summary: Dynamic in-air handover is hard for dual-arm robots because it needs accurate perception, tight coordination and natural motion. Prior methods relied on dynamics models, strong priors or depth sensors. This work trains an end-to-end policy with multi-agent RL from RGB images alone, plus a human-policy regularizer for fluid throwing. In Isaac Sim it reaches about 99% success on training objects and 75% on unseen ones.
conclusion_summary: Presented as the first end-to-end RGB-only framework for dual-arm in-air handover, producing human-like throw and catch without explicit dynamics or depth. The authors warn that sim-to-real gaps could create safety risks on real robots; future work adds safety mechanisms and better generalization.

title: DeReCo: Decoupling Representation and Coordination Learning for Object-Adaptive Decentralized Multi-Robot Cooperative Transport
authors: Shibata, Sota, Bosch, Kadokawa, Tsurumine, Matsubara
abstract_summary: Learning object representations from partial observations and learning coordination under changing teammate policies interfere with each other when trained together. DeReCo separates them in three stages: centralized coordination learning with privileged object information, supervised reconstruction of object representations from local observations, then removal of the privileged information for decentralized execution. It beats baselines on three training objects, generalizes to six unseen objects, and wins on two unseen objects with two real HSR robots.
conclusion_summary: Decoupling makes multi-agent RL training more stable and sample-efficient. Tests on nine object shapes (six unseen) and real-robot runs confirm transfer from simulation. Future work covers a wider range of object properties and larger teams.

title: Two are not always better than one: Role specialization is an important determinant of collaborative task performance
authors: Takai, Fu, Doibata, Lisi, Tsuchiya, Mojtahedi, Yoshioka, Kawato, Morimoto, Santello
abstract_summary: Participants moved a virtual beam using two robotic handles, alone with both hands or in pairs, with symmetric or asymmetric pivot setups. Pairs beat solo participants only in the asymmetric setup, where one hand naturally led and used more force. In the symmetric setup solo participants did better and contributions were roughly equal.
conclusion_summary: Having a partner helps only when distinct roles emerge. Without roles, paired performance was less stable, slower and needed more trials. Roles let each person focus on a manageable sub-task instead of synchronizing equal contributions. The authors suggest brain-imaging follow-ups. Relevant to "one holds, one unscrews": asymmetry may be what makes teamwork pay off.
note: Human study, not a robot paper.

title: RoCo: Dialectic Multi-Robot Collaboration with Large Language Models
abstract_summary: Each robot is paired with an LLM that discusses task strategy with the other robots. The result is sub-tasks plus 3D waypoint paths, which a multi-arm motion planner turns into trajectories. Environment feedback such as collision checks lets the agents revise plans. The authors release RoCoBench, a six-task benchmark with a text dataset, and report high success rates. Real-world tests show a human can join the dialog.
conclusion_summary: LLMs can handle both coordination and planning across robots. The benchmark will be open-sourced. Results suggest broad applicability and adaptation to task variations with few or no examples; limitations and improvements are acknowledged.

title: MHRC: Closed-loop Decentralized Multi-Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration with Large Language Models
authors: Yu, Peng, Ying, Li, Ji, Zhang
abstract_summary: LLMs let mobile, manipulation and mobile-manipulation robots collaborate with no central controller on exploration, transport and organization tasks. Textual feedback and chain-of-thought prompting support planning, and the mobile manipulator can reposition its base for better grasps. PyBullet tests across three room layouts and ablations show the modules help.
conclusion_summary: Decentralized collaboration among heterogeneous robots works through LLMs, and robot-type-specific feedback enables replanning from real-time results, improving success in simulation. Future work: more robot types (legged, drones) and fewer redundant actions.

title: SayCoNav: LLMs for Adaptive Collaboration in Decentralized Multi-Robot Navigation
abstract_summary: An LLM designs a collaboration strategy for the team, then each robot plans and acts on its own with an LLM. Robots share information while navigating and keep revising plans. On Multi-Object Navigation tasks, search efficiency improved by up to 44.28% over baselines, and the system adapts to changing conditions mid-mission.
conclusion_summary: The strategy can be regenerated when a robot's condition changes, so each robot's strengths stay in use. Experiments across team compositions show it works for large unknown spaces. Limitation: tasks needing tight coordination, such as finding tiny objects in closed containers. Real-robot tests are planned.

title: LLM-Guided Decentralized Exploration with Self-Organizing Robot Teams
abstract_summary: Robots with limited sensing or fault tolerance should form teams while exploring without a central controller. The authors combine autonomous dynamic team formation with LLM-based selection of each team's next target, as an alternative to frontier-based and RL methods. Validated in simulation with tens to hundreds of robots.
conclusion_summary: The method beat a baseline that samples frontier cells probabilistically, and large swarms with team-level LLM reasoning explored efficiently. Future work: limited communication, adjusting team sizes, and tasks like object transport.

title: LLM2Swarm: Robot Swarms that Responsively Reason, Plan, and Collaborate through LLMs
abstract_summary: Swarm controllers are usually hand-written, which is slow and limited to anticipated situations. The paper proposes indirect integration (LLMs generate and check controller code) and direct integration (each robot runs an LLM to reason, plan and communicate in natural language). Simulated showcases show robots detecting anomalies without being told what they are. Mostly conceptual; software and videos released.
conclusion_summary: LLMs let swarm robots communicate in natural language with each other and with human operators, easing controller generation, raising autonomy and opening new human-swarm interaction. Technical challenges remain, but the authors expect LLM-enabled swarms to change swarm robotics.

title: Distributed Formation Shape Control of Identity-less Robot Swarms
abstract_summary: Identical robots form a shape without unique labels. A formation description that does not depend on identities, plus a distributed negotiation, lets robots agree on the shape's position and orientation. A fully distributed control law uses only locally sensed information and handles static shapes and ones that translate, rotate or deform. Simulations and Crazyflie drone flights show robustness, including when robots are added or removed.
conclusion_summary: Robots take a graphical shape as input, negotiate its Euclidean parameters locally, and form the shape while negotiating. Simulations with up to 200 robots and a 7-drone experiment suggest convergence time grows only mildly with swarm size. Future work: noise, obstacles, communication delay and role switching.

title: Self-Healing Distributed Swarm Formation Control Using Image Moments
authors: Liu, Donato Ridgley, Elwin, Rubenstein, Freeman, Lynch
abstract_summary: Image moments give a compact, low-dimensional way for a person to describe a formation. Each robot estimates the swarm's current moments through a distributed process while steering toward the desired ones. No central controller, fixed message size regardless of swarm size, and recovery from errors, packet loss, and robots joining or leaving. 50 robots reached the desired formations despite nearly 50% packet loss.
conclusion_summary: A scalable, self-healing method where the number of moments sets the level of formation detail. Gain selection for coupled estimation and control needs more study; smaller gains on higher-order moments generally converged better. Distributed model predictive control is suggested to speed convergence.

title: Meanshift Shape Formation Control Using Discrete Mass Distribution
authors: Cai, Gao, Li, Wang, Sun, Lü
abstract_summary: Density-based control handles changing swarm size but struggles with complex shapes and decentralized operation. Here the target shape is a mass distribution over discrete sample points. Each robot estimates sample-point masses locally, and a decentralized meanshift controller pulls the swarm toward that distribution. Simulations and real robots show efficient formation of complex shapes and adaptation to swarm-size changes.
conclusion_summary: Three parts (discrete mass model, decentralized estimator, meanshift controller) work together. Stability is established and convergence is proven for convex shapes. Future work: an estimator that needs no broadcast when robots are removed, and larger real-world swarms.

title: RSC: Decentralized Rigid Formation Flocking for Large-Scale Swarms via Hybrid Predictive Control and Online Reconfiguration
abstract_summary: Existing methods for keeping a rigid shape while moving often hit local minima, oscillate, or fail around obstacles. RSC combines finite-horizon trajectory prediction with a reactive potential-field safety controller, and exchanges leader-follower roles online to restore the formation after obstacles. With 25 UAVs in clutter it reaches an 83% success rate under strict criteria versus below 5% for baselines.
conclusion_summary: Predictive planning, reactive safety control and dynamic topology reconfiguration balance long-term coordination with short-term collision avoidance, addressing deadlocks and local minima. Suggested uses: payload transport and communication relays underground. Future work: moving obstacles, degraded communication, and structures more flexible than leader-follower.

title: LLM-Flock: Decentralized Multi-Robot Flocking via Large Language Models and Influence-Based Consensus
abstract_summary: Robots that each plan with their own LLM often behave unpredictably, bunching or scattering. In LLM-Flock each robot generates a formation plan and refines it by adopting plans from more influential neighbors. Simulations with several LLMs and Crazyflie tests show better stability, convergence and adaptability than earlier LLM approaches.
conclusion_summary: Per-robot LLM planning plus influence-based consensus gives stable, scalable decentralized flocking with no central control or retraining, including on real drones. The consensus step reduces inconsistencies in unstructured LLM reasoning. Pairing language models with lightweight coordination looks promising.

title: Decentralized Adaptive Formation via Consensus-Oriented Multi-Agent Communication
abstract_summary: Keeping a formation as the number of agents changes is hard, especially with limited communication. In Cons-DecAF, a multi-agent RL method (ConsMAC) lets agents build a shared picture of the global situation by combining neighbors' messages. Policy distillation handles adaptive adjustment, and a Hausdorff-distance-based displacement replaces fixed position assignments. Simulations show strong speed and stability.
note: Conclusion not summarized: only the abstract was retrieved.

title: Communicating Plans, Not Percepts: Scalable Multi-Agent Coordination with Embodied World Models
abstract_summary: Two cooperating agents in a partially observable grid world communicate in one of two ways: a message protocol learned end-to-end from reward alone, or messages compressed from each agent's world-model rollout of its own planned path. The world-model approach performed better, learned more efficiently and scaled to larger grids.
conclusion_summary: The learned protocol coordinated in simple settings but failed to scale to larger, more partially observable ones. The world-model approach kept near-perfect success as complexity grew. The authors argue explicit predictive models should be central to communication in embodied AI. Future work: stochastic world models, physical robots, adaptive communication, larger teams.
